title: Episode 247: Sam Houston: San Jacinto, the Lone Star Republic, and the Union Defiant
description:
The larger-than-life epic of Sam Houston: living with the Cherokees, fighting alongside Andrew Jackson at Horseshoe Bend, winning Texas independence in eighteen minutes at San Jacinto, serving as President of Texas, and sacrificing his office to defend the Union against secession.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. Today, our chronicle of the Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans explores the colossal, colorful, and fiercely principled frontiersman who won the independence of Texas and stood alone to defend the American Union: General Sam Houston.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE CHEROKEE BROTHER: THE RAVEN OF HIWASSEE ISLAND
Born in 1793 in the Shenandoah Valley of Virginia, Sam Houston was a rebellious, independent youth who moved with his widowed mother to the rugged frontier of eastern Tennessee. Refusing to work as a store clerk or plow his family's farm, sixteen-year-old Sam vanished into the wilderness, crossing the Tennessee River to live with the Cherokee people on Hiwassee Island. Adopted by Cherokee Chief Oolooteka, young Houston lived among the Cherokees for three years, becoming fluent in their language, wearing native dress, learning tribal customs, and receiving the Cherokee name Colonneh, meaning 'The Raven'. Houston later declared: 'I'd rather be a wild Indian than a civilized slave; I loved their liberty, their wild sports, their dances, and their woodcraft.' In 1813, Houston enlisted as a private in the United States Army during the Creek War, marching under General Andrew Jackson. At the bloody Battle of Horseshoe Bend in March 1814, Houston mounted the Creek wooden breastwork under heavy fire, an arrow striking him in the groin and two musket balls shattering his shoulder. Jackson witnessed his extraordinary courage, forming a lifelong father-son bond that launched Houston's soaring political career in Tennessee.  Houston's Cherokee mentor Chief Oolooteka stood six feet six inches tall, instilling in the young Virginian an appreciation for physical courage, native eloquence, and outdoor endurance.  Houston's mother Elizabeth Paxton Houston had handed him his father's musket when he enlisted in 1813, telling him: 'Take this musket and never disgrace it; for my door is always open to a brave boy, but shut to a coward.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE GOVERNOR'S SCANDAL AND THE RETURN TO THE BLANKET
Backed by Andrew Jackson, Houston's political rise in Tennessee was meteoric: he became district attorney, major general of the militia, United States congressman, and in 1827, at age thirty-four, was elected Governor of Tennessee. He seemed destined for the presidency. But in January 1829, Houston married twenty-year-old Eliza Allen, daughter of a prominent aristocratic Tennessee family. Eleven weeks later, the marriage collapsed in absolute, mysterious secrecy amidst rumors of a private incompatibility that Houston gentlemanly refused to explain for the rest of his life. Facing public scandal and political ruin, Houston resigned the governorship, gave up his political career, boarded a steamboat on the Cumberland River, and vanished into the western Indian Territory, present-day Oklahoma. Rejoining Chief Oolooteka and his Cherokee brethren, Houston 'returned to the blanket', drinking heavily to drown his sorrows—earning the tragic Cherokee nickname 'Big Drunk'—and marrying a Cherokee woman named Tiana Rogers. In 1832, wearing buckskins and Indian blankets, Houston traveled to Washington to expose corrupt federal Indian agents who were starving displaced tribes, engaging in a celebrated street fight with an Ohio congressman where Houston beat him with a hickory cane. Andrew Jackson intervened, giving his troubled protégé a new mission: go to Mexican Texas to report on conditions among the American settlers.  During his exile in the Indian Territory, Houston represented Cherokee chiefs in treaty negotiations, fighting corrupt federal contractors who provided spoiled flour and rotten pork to displaced families.  Houston's friendship with Jackson remained unbreakable: when Jackson was dying at the Hermitage in 1845, Houston rushed to his bedside with his infant son, arriving hours after the old general had passed away.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE ALAMO AND THE RUNAWAY SCRAPE: MARCH 1836
Arriving in Texas in 1832, Houston found a land on the brink of armed rebellion against the centralist dictatorship of Mexican General Antonio López de Santa Anna. In March 1836, at Washington-on-the-Brazos, the delegates declared the independence of the Republic of Texas and appointed Sam Houston as Commander-in-Chief of the Texas Army. Days later, catastrophic news arrived: the Alamo in San Antonio had fallen; its one hundred and eighty-nine defenders, including Davy Crockett and William Barret Travis, had been butchered to the last man. Soon after, four hundred Texas prisoners under James Fannin were massacred in cold blood at Goliad by Santa Anna's orders. While panic-stricken settlers fled toward Louisiana in the chaos known as the 'Runaway Scrape', Houston's green army of four hundred volunteers wanted to charge into suicidal battle against Santa Anna's four thousand veteran Mexican troops. Houston held his nerve, ordering a month-long strategic retreat through driving spring rains, burning towns, and swollen rivers, drilling his men and waiting with iron patience for the overconfident Santa Anna to divide his forces and make a fatal mistake.  During the Runaway Scrape, Houston's patience was tested by his own officers who accused him of cowardice, but Houston calmly replied, 'I consult no one; I will fight when I am ready.'  At San Jacinto, Houston's tactical restraint in waiting for the Mexican afternoon siesta was praised by military historians as a textbook example of asymmetric frontier warfare.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE BATTLE OF SAN JACINTO: EIGHTEEN MINUTES OF DESTINY: APRIL 21, 1836
On April 20, 1836, Santa Anna led a vanguard of nine hundred Mexican soldiers onto the coastal plain of San Jacinto, near present-day Houston, camping with his back against Buffalo Bayou and the San Jacinto marshland. Houston positioned his nine hundred Texans in a grove of live oaks, concealed by tall coastal grass. On the morning of April 21, Houston dispatched scout Deaf Smith to chop down Vince's Bridge, cutting off the only avenue of retreat for both armies. At three-thirty in the afternoon, during the Mexican army's traditional siesta, Houston ordered the attack. With the fife and drum playing a popular love song, 'Will You Come to the Bower?', the Texans advanced silently across the open prairie. When they were within seventy yards of the Mexican barricades, Houston drew his broadsword and shouted the battle cries: 'Remember the Alamo! Remember Goliad!' The surprise was total. The Texans shattered the Mexican breastworks in a ferocious charge: within eighteen minutes, the battle was decided. Mexican soldiers broke in blind panic into the marshes; six hundred and thirty Mexican soldiers were killed, seven hundred and thirty captured, while the Texans lost just nine men. Houston's horse was shot out from under him, and a musket ball shattered his left ankle, his boot filling with blood.  The Battle of San Jacinto remains one of the most decisive battles in world history, paving the way for the American acquisition of Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, Nevada, Utah, and California.  The Treaties of Velasco signed by Santa Anna established the Rio Grande as the southern and western boundary of Texas, a disputed border that later sparked the Mexican-American War in 1846.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: CAPTURING SANTA ANNA AND THE BIRTH OF THE LONE STAR REPUBLIC
The day after the battle, Texas scouts captured a Mexican soldier dressed in a common private's blue smock and red slippers, hiding in the tall grass. When he was brought to the Texas camp, Mexican prisoners saluted him, crying out: 'El Presidente! El Presidente!' It was General Santa Anna himself. Lying on a blanket beneath a giant live oak tree, his shattered ankle throbbing with agony, General Houston conducted the historic surrender negotiation. While enraged Texas soldiers surrounded the tree shouting for Santa Anna to be hanged on the spot for the massacres at the Alamo and Goliad, Houston preserved the dictator's life, recognizing that Santa Anna was worth far more alive than dead. Houston forced Santa Anna to sign the Treaties of Velasco, ordering all remaining Mexican armies to withdraw beyond the Rio Grande and recognizing the independence of the Republic of Texas. In October 1836, Sam Houston was elected the first constitutional President of the Republic of Texas, establishing the capital of the young Lone Star nation in the new frontier town named in his honor.  Houston's treatment of Santa Anna was praised by European diplomats for its chivalric magnanimity, proving that the frontier general was a civilized statesman of the highest order.  As Senator from Texas, Houston was the only southern senator to vote for every part of the Compromise of 1850 and the only one to vote against the Kansas-Nebraska Act, predicting it would destroy the South.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE PRESIDENT AND THE ANNEXATION OF TEXAS: 1845
As President of the Republic of Texas for two terms, Houston demonstrated extraordinary statesmanlike pragmatism: he balanced the bankrupt Texas budget, established peaceful treaties with the Comanche and Cherokee tribes, and successfully defended the frontier against Mexican incursions. Houston's ultimate strategic goal was the annexation of Texas into the United States. Playing a brilliant diplomatic game, Houston flirted with British and French diplomats, hinting that Texas might become a British protectorate, which panicked Washington into action. In December 1845, Texas was admitted as the twenty-eighth state of the American Union, with Houston elected as one of its first United States Senators. In Washington, wearing a leopard-skin waistcoat and Mexican serape over his suit, carving small wooden hearts with a pocketknife during Senate debates, Houston stood with Henry Clay and Daniel Webster to champion the Compromise of 1850, fiercely opposing southern disunion.  Houston's beloved third wife Margaret Lea Houston, a devout Baptist from Alabama, helped him conquer his drinking problems and supported his principled political crusades with steadfast devotion.  Houston's famous warning against secession was delivered from the balcony of the Tremont House hotel in Galveston, facing down an armed, hostile mob with towering physical courage.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE UNION DEFIANT: THE REFUSAL OF THE CONFEDERATE OATH: 1861
In 1859, Sam Houston was elected Governor of Texas, the only man in American history to serve as governor of two different states. In 1861, following the election of Abraham Lincoln, a wave of secessionist hysteria swept Texas. Houston stood practically alone against the tide, touring the state to deliver blistering speeches warning his fellow Texans of the catastrophe they were bringing upon themselves: 'Let me tell you what is coming. After the sacrifice of countless millions of treasure and hundreds of thousands of lives, you may win southern independence, but I doubt it. The North can make a foot of movement to your foot of progress; they can send ten men to your one; the North can manufacture all its munitions of war. You may win a few victories, but your people will be sacrificed and your property confiscated.' On March 16, 1861, the Texas Secession Convention commanded all state officials to take the oath of allegiance to the Confederacy. When the secretary called Houston's name three times in the state capitol, the sixty-eight-year-old governor sat upstairs in his office, quietly whittling a piece of pine wood. He refused to appear, declaring that he loved Texas too well to bring civil war upon her people, and surrendered his governorship rather than betray the United States Constitution. Sam Houston died in Huntsville, Texas, in July 1863, with the sounds of Civil War echoing across the continent, his final dying whisper: 'Texas. Texas. Margaret.' Sam Houston stood as a colossal giant of the American continent, who gave Texas its liberty and gave America his undivided loyalty.  When Texas seceded, President Lincoln sent a confidential courier offering Houston fifty thousand federal troops to keep Texas in the Union by force, but Houston refused, wishing to avoid fratricidal war.  Today, the monumental sixty-seven-foot white statue of Sam Houston, 'A Tribute to Courage', stands tall along Interstate 45 in Huntsville, honoring the father of Texas and the defender of the Union.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our Top 50 Non-President Americans series continues with Episode 248: Davy Crockett—The King of the Wild Frontier, the Bear Hunter in Congress, and the Alamo. Until then, stay curious.
